summary: Describes data types and algorithms that make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as Structured Fields. It is meant for specifications of new HTTP fields. It obsoletes RFC 8941.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP headers carry small pieces of information, and every header has traditionally had its own slightly different way of being written. This document defines a common way to write them, using a small set of types such as lists, dictionaries, numbers, strings and dates. A field that uses these rules can be read and written by one generic program, so a new header costs nothing extra to handle.

questions: how to parse structured field values
how are structured field values parsed
what types do structured fields support
subtitle: A common set of data types for HTTP header and trailer fields, so that each new field does not need its own parser.

tldr.problem: Writing the syntax of a new HTTP header field is full of pitfalls, and once the field exists each implementation often has to write its own parser and serializer for it.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines three top-level types, List, Dictionary and Item, with a fixed set of item types, and gives step-by-step algorithms for turning a field value into a structure and back again.
tldr.outcome: Any field that opts in can be handled by one generic parser. The format is deliberately strict, so a malformed value fails the whole field rather than being half-understood, which is what keeps two implementations in step.

today: RFC 9651 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of Structured Field Values for HTTP. It replaced RFC 8941, which defined the same List, Dictionary and Item model without the Date and Display String types.

sections.title: Why HTTP Needs Structured Fields
sections.content:
Specifying the syntax of a new HTTP header or trailer field is an onerous task; even with the guidance in Section 16.3.2 of the HTTP specification, there are many decisions and pitfalls for a prospective field author.

Once a field is defined, bespoke parsers and serializers often need to be written, because each field value has a slightly different handling of what looks like common syntax.

This document introduces a set of common data structures for use in definitions of new HTTP field values. In particular, it defines a generic, abstract model for them, along with a concrete serialization for expressing that model in HTTP header and trailer fields. A field defined as a Structured Header or Structured Trailer, or a Structured Field that can be either, uses the types defined here to define its syntax and basic handling rules, thereby simplifying both its definition by specification writers and its handling by implementations.

Additionally, future versions of HTTP can define alternative serializations of the abstract model of these structures, allowing fields that use that model to be transmitted more efficiently without being redefined. It is not a goal of this document to redefine the syntax of existing HTTP fields; the mechanisms described here are only intended to be used with fields that explicitly opt into them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new HTTP header used to bring its own tiny dialect along. This document gives header authors a shared vocabulary to pick from, and implementation authors one parser that already knows how to read it.

sections.title: Strict Processing on Purpose
sections.content:
This specification intentionally defines strict parsing and serialization behaviours using step-by-step algorithms; the only error handling defined is to fail the entire operation altogether.

It is designed to encourage faithful implementation and good interoperability. An implementation that tried to be helpful by being more tolerant of input would make interoperability worse, since that would create pressure on other implementations to implement similar, but likely subtly different, workarounds.

In other words, strict processing is an intentional feature of this specification; it allows non-conformant input to be discovered and corrected by the producer early and avoids both interoperability and security issues that might otherwise result. As a result of this strictness, if a field is appended to by multiple parties, such as intermediaries or different components in the sender, an error in one party's value is likely to cause the entire field value to fail parsing.

The document also uses algorithms to specify parsing and serialization behaviours. When parsing from HTTP fields, implementations MUST have behaviour that is indistinguishable from following the algorithms. For serialization, the algorithms define the recommended way to produce the fields, and implementations MAY vary from the specified behaviour so long as the output is still correctly handled by the parsing algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The format refuses anything it does not fully understand rather than guessing. That sounds unhelpful, but two programs that guess differently would disagree about the same message, and a sender that gets an error can fix its own code straight away.

sections.title: What Happens When a Field Fails to Parse
sections.content:
When parsing fails, the entire field is ignored. Field definitions cannot override this because doing so would preclude handling by generic software; they can only add additional constraints, for example on the numeric range of Integers and Decimals, the format of Strings and Tokens, the types allowed in a Dictionary's values, or the number of Items in a List.

When field-specific constraints are violated, the entire field is also ignored, unless the field definition defines other handling requirements. For example, if a header field is defined as an Item and required to be an Integer, but a String is received, it should be ignored unless that field's definition explicitly specifies otherwise.

Structured Fields are designed to be extensible because experience has shown that, even when it is not foreseen, it is often necessary to modify and add to the allowable syntax and semantics of a field in a controlled fashion. Both Items and Inner Lists allow Parameters as an extensibility mechanism, so that their values can later be extended to accommodate more information. To preserve forward compatibility, field specifications are discouraged from defining the presence of an unrecognized parameter as an error condition.

Field specifications are required to be either an Item, List or Dictionary to preserve extensibility. Fields that erroneously defined as another type, such as Integer, are assumed to be Items, and so allow Parameters. A field definition can specify that grease parameters be added by senders, which helps to discourage recipients from writing a parser that does not account for Parameters. Specifications that use Dictionaries can also allow for forward compatibility by requiring that the presence of, as well as the value and type associated with, unknown keys be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: If a field cannot be read, the whole field is dropped, not partly used. The extra key-value pairs called parameters are the escape hatch: a field can grow new parameters later, and readers that do not know one must ignore it rather than reject the field.

sections.title: The Structured Data Types
sections.content:
There are three top-level types that an HTTP field can be defined as: Lists, Dictionaries and Items. Lists and Dictionaries are containers; their members can be Items or Inner Lists, which are themselves arrays of Items. Both Items and Inner Lists can be parameterized with key/value pairs.

A List is an array of zero or more members, each of which can be an Item or an Inner List. An empty List is denoted by not serializing the field at all, which implies that fields defined as Lists have a default empty value. When serialized as a textual HTTP field, each member is separated by a comma and optional whitespace, as in Example-List: sugar, tea, rum. Parsers MUST support Lists containing at least 1024 members.

An Inner List is an array of zero or more Items. Both the individual Items and the Inner List itself can be parameterized. When serialized in a textual HTTP field, Inner Lists are denoted by surrounding parenthesis and their values are delimited by one or more spaces, as in Example-List: ("foo" "bar"), ("baz"), ("bat" "one"), (). Parsers MUST support Inner Lists containing at least 256 members.

A Dictionary is an ordered map of key-value pairs, where the keys are short textual strings and the values are Items or arrays of Items. As with Lists, an empty Dictionary is represented by omitting the entire field. Recipients MUST ignore members whose keys are undefined or unknown, unless the field's specification specifically disallows them. Parsers MUST support Dictionaries containing at least 1024 key/value pairs and keys with at least 64 characters.

Parameters are an ordered map of key-value pairs associated with an Item or Inner List. The keys are unique within their scope, and the values are bare items, which cannot themselves be parameterized. Parsers MUST support at least 256 parameters on an Item or Inner List, and support parameter keys with at least 64 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three shapes a field can have. A list is a row of values. A dictionary is a row of named values. An item is a single value. Lists and items can carry extra named settings, and a list can contain small sub-lists written in brackets.

sections.title: How Each Kind of Value Is Written
sections.content:
An Item can be an Integer, a Decimal, a String, a Token, a Byte Sequence, a Boolean or a Date, and it can have associated parameters.

Integers have a range of -999,999,999,999,999 to 999,999,999,999,999 inclusive, that is, up to fifteen digits, signed, for IEEE 754 compatibility. Decimals are numbers with an integer and a fractional component, where the integer component has at most 12 digits and the fractional component at most three digits. The serialization algorithm rounds input with more than three digits of precision in the fractional component.

Strings are zero or more printable ASCII characters, that is the range %x20 to %x7E, which excludes tabs, newlines and carriage returns. When serialized, Strings are delimited with double quotes, using a backslash to escape double quotes and backslashes. Only DQUOTE and backslash can be escaped; other characters after a backslash MUST cause parsing to fail. Parsers MUST support Strings, after any decoding, with at least 1024 characters.

Tokens are short textual words that begin with an alphabetic character or an asterisk, followed by zero to many token characters, which are the same as those allowed by the token rule in HTTP plus the colon and slash characters. Parsers MUST support Tokens with at least 512 characters. Tokens are defined largely for compatibility with the data model of existing HTTP fields, so new fields are encouraged to use Strings.

A Byte Sequence is delimited with colons and encoded using base64, and parsers MUST support Byte Sequences with at least 16384 octets after decoding. A Boolean is indicated with a leading question mark followed by a 1 for true or a 0 for false. In Dictionary and Parameter values, Boolean true is indicated by omitting the value.

Dates have a data model similar to Integers, representing a possibly negative delta in seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, excluding leap seconds, and are serialized with a leading at sign. Parsers MUST support Dates whose values include all days in years 1 to 9999. Display Strings are similar to Strings but allow Unicode scalar values, and are intended for cases where a value is displayed to end users. In textual HTTP fields they are represented in a manner similar to Strings, except that non-ASCII characters are percent-encoded, with a leading percent sign to distinguish them from Strings.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of value has one way of being written. Numbers have limits on how long they may be. Text that is not plain ASCII has to be escaped, either as a percent-encoded display string or as a string of bytes in base64. Dates are just a number of seconds with a marker in front.

sections.title: Serializing and Parsing
sections.content:
Serializing turns a structure into an ASCII string suitable for use in an HTTP field value. If the structure is a Dictionary or List and its value is empty, the field is not serialized at all, so both the field name and the field value are omitted. Otherwise the appropriate algorithm for a List, a Dictionary or an Item is run, and the result is returned converted into an array of bytes using ASCII encoding. Any other case fails serialization.

Parsing goes the other way. Given an array of bytes representing the field's value, which is empty if the field is not present, and the field type, which is dictionary, list or item, the algorithm converts the bytes to an ASCII string, discards leading spaces, runs the algorithm for that type, discards leading spaces again, and fails parsing if anything is left over.

When generating the input bytes, parsers MUST combine all field lines in the same section that case-insensitively match the field name into one comma-separated field value, so that the entire field value is processed correctly. Lists and Dictionaries can have their members split across multiple lines of the same section, but individual members cannot be safely split between lines. Strings split across multiple field lines will have unpredictable results, because one or more commas with optional whitespace will become part of the string output. Tokens, Integers, Decimals and Byte Sequences cannot be split across multiple field lines, because the inserted commas will cause parsing to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing is the reverse of reading. A field with nothing in it is left out entirely rather than sent empty, and everything after the value has been read must be blank, otherwise the field is rejected.

sections.title: IANA Registration and What Changed from RFC 8941
sections.content:
IANA has added a Structured Type column to the HTTP Field Name Registry. The column indicates the type of the field, if any, and may be Dictionary, List or Item. A note records that field names beginning with characters other than ALPHA or an asterisk will not be able to be represented as a Structured Fields Token and therefore may be incompatible with being mapped into field values that refer to it. The type for each existing registry entry listed in the document's table has also been added, covering fields such as Accept-CH, Cache-Status, CDN-Cache-Control, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, Origin-Agent-Cluster, Priority and Proxy-Status.

This revision of the specification has made the following changes from RFC 8941: it added the Date Structured Type; stopped encouraging the use of ABNF in definitions of new Structured Fields and moved the ABNF to an informative appendix; added a Structured Type column to the HTTP Field Name Registry; refined parse failure handling; and added the Display String Structured Type.

The document is also backward compatible with RFC 8941: a parser that implements the requirements here can also parse valid Structured Fields whose definitions reference RFC 8941. Upgrading an implementation to support a newer revision brings the possibility that some field values that were invalid according to the earlier RFC might become valid, because a value that the older parser rejected, such as a syntactically valid Date in a field that did not accommodate Dates, may now parse.
sections.plainLanguage: The main additions since the previous version are a date type and a type for text meant to be shown to people, and a registry column that records which type each HTTP header uses. The format stays compatible with the old one, so an old parser and a new one can still talk to each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The size of most types defined by Structured Fields is not limited, so extremely large fields could be an attack vector, for example for resource consumption. Most HTTP implementations limit the sizes of individual fields as well as the overall header or trailer section size to mitigate such attacks.

It is possible for parties with the ability to inject new HTTP fields to change the meaning of a Structured Field. In some circumstances this will cause parsing to fail, but it is not possible to reliably fail in all such circumstances.

The Display String type can convey any possible Unicode code point without sanitization; for example, they might contain unassigned code points, control points including NUL, or noncharacters. Applications consuming Display Strings therefore need to consider strategies such as filtering or escaping untrusted content before displaying it.
sections.plainLanguage: Three risks are named here. A field can be made enormous to exhaust the reader's memory. A middlebox can add a field and change the meaning of another. And a display string can carry any character at all, including control characters, so a program showing it to a person has to filter it first.

items.label: Integer
items.desc: Up to fifteen signed digits, from -999,999,999,999,999 to 999,999,999,999,999.

items.label: Decimal
items.desc: At most 12 digits before the point and 3 after it.

items.label: String
items.desc: Printable ASCII in double quotes, with backslash escapes.

items.label: Token
items.desc: A short word starting with a letter or an asterisk.

items.label: Boolean
items.desc: A question mark followed by 1 for true or 0 for false.

items.label: Display String
items.desc: A percent sign, then a quoted string with non-ASCII characters percent-encoded.

viz.caption: ABNF OF STRUCTURED FIELDS, FROM THE INFORMATIVE APPENDIX

data.title: Structured Fields grammar
data.code:
sf-list       = list-member *( OWS "," OWS list-member )
list-member   = sf-item / inner-list

inner-list    = "(" *SP [ sf-item *( 1*SP sf-item ) *SP ] ")"
               parameters

parameters    = *( ";" *SP parameter )
parameter     = param-key [ "=" param-value ]

sf-dictionary = dict-member *( OWS "," OWS dict-member )
dict-member  = member-key ( parameters / ( "=" member-value ))

sf-item       = bare-item parameters
bare-item     = sf-integer / sf-decimal / sf-string / sf-token
               / sf-binary / sf-boolean / sf-date / sf-displaystring

sf-integer       = ["-"] 1*15DIGIT
sf-decimal       = ["-"] 1*12DIGIT "." 1*3DIGIT
sf-string        = DQUOTE *( unescaped / "%" / bs-escaped ) DQUOTE
sf-token         = ( ALPHA / "*" ) *( tchar / ":" / "/" )
sf-binary        = ":" base64 ":"
sf-boolean       = "?" ( "0" / "1" )
sf-date          = "@" sf-integer
sf-displaystring = "%" DQUOTE *( unescaped / "\" / pct-encoded )
                  DQUOTE

viz.caption: THE THREE RISKS THE DOCUMENT NAMES

items.title: Unbounded size
items.text: Most types have no size limit, so a huge field can be used to exhaust the reader's resources.

items.title: Injected fields
items.text: A party able to add HTTP fields can change the meaning of a Structured Field.

items.title: Display Strings
items.text: They can carry any Unicode code point, so untrusted content should be filtered or escaped before display.
